sources: Campbell, J. F. Popular Tales of the West Highlands. Vol. III. Edinburgh: Edmonston and Douglas, 1862, 81.
Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989. Pp. 27, 139.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The boar is a symbolic animal. Art and coins from insular and continental sources picture it. It was the most savage animal the ancient Celts met. It became a sign of raw force, firm endurance, and sexual power. Its meat was often part of the Champion's Portion. Its skin made warriors' cloaks. Its favored meat also made it a sign of prosperity. On the Isle of Man the Arkan Sonney, called the lucky piggy, was a lovely white fairy pig. People held that it brought luck. The boar appears in major Irish legend cycles. The hero Diarmait Ua Duibine died after killing one. He stepped on a poisonous bristle while measuring the beast. An Otherworld pig could be eaten yet endlessly restore its flesh. In the Mabinogion, boars come from the Otherworld.

okr.objective: Describe the boar as a symbolic animal of strength and prosperity.
